idiom_name: case object extending the trait (Nil and None are the standard library's own)
implementation_notes: Scala implements the pattern inside its own collections: Nil is a case object extending List[Nothing] that supports every List method (map, head, fold and cons all have defined benign answers), and None is a case object extending Option[Nothing] whose combinators are total. User code mirrors it with a case object - `case object Unknown extends Customer` - that overrides the contract with domain defaults, ideally inside a sealed trait so a `match` is exhaustive without a wildcard. Option itself still forces the caller to handle emptiness, so the two halves of the decision are: Option for optional results, a case object when the empty value should keep answering.
pitfalls: A case object in a sealed hierarchy must live in the same file as the trait (or its companion), otherwise the hierarchy stops being sealed and exhaustiveness checking is lost.
Option.get, head and similar partial methods throw on None/Nil: the special case must be total, because callers were promised they no longer need to test.
null still enters through Java interop, and a null returned by a Java API is not Unknown - it is a NullPointerException before the pattern can help.
Case objects are serializable singletons: adding fields to a case object later breaks deserialisation of previously written values (readResolve equality).
